title: A curve, a tangent, a better question.
subtitle: An interactive field guide to local and finite change.

pages.title: The slope belongs to a point.
pages.summary: A derivative describes how a curve changes right here. A tangent makes that local rate visible.

blocks.title: Start with a family of curves
blocks.text: Our example is f(x) = a × x². The parameter a changes the height and steepness. The marked point stays at x = 1; its height is a.

blocks.title: Ask for the local slope
blocks.text: The derivative is f′(x) = 2ax. At the marked point, f′(1) = 2a. This is the instantaneous rate at x = 1, not the exact rise of the curve over a whole unit step.

blocks.title: Draw the local linear model
blocks.text: The tangent passes through (1, a) and has slope 2a. Its equation is L(x) = a + 2a(x − 1). Close to the marked point, it provides a linear approximation to the curve.

steps.text: Start at the marked point. With a equal to {a}, x is one and the curve has height {y}. Change the parameter and notice how that height changes.
At x equals one, the derivative is two times a, so the local slope is {slope}. This number describes the slope at the point. It is not the curve's exact rise from one to two.
The tangent keeps that local slope. It starts at height {y} when x is one. At x equals two it reaches {tangentEndY}. We will compare that prediction with the curve on the next page.

quickQuestions: Draw the tangent and explain its slope at x = 1.
Why is the derivative 2a? Show the short derivation.
Set a to 3 and explain what changed.

quiz.question: For f(x) = x², what does f′(1) = 2 describe?

options.text: The exact rise of the curve from x = 1 to x = 2.
A constant slope everywhere on the curve.

quiz.explanation: The derivative gives a local rate. The exact curve rise from 1 to 2 is 4 − 1 = 3, and the curve's slope changes with x.

pages.title: A finite step tells a different story.
pages.summary: Keep the interval fixed. Compare what the curve does with what its tangent predicts.

blocks.title: Calculate the curve's exact rise
blocks.text: From x = 1 to x = 2, the curve moves from a to 4a. Its exact change is 3a. This is a finite unit interval, not an infinitesimal step.

blocks.title: Calculate the tangent's rise
blocks.text: Over the same interval, the tangent moves from a to 3a, a change of 2a. That is an exact change for the tangent line and only a prediction for the curve.

blocks.title: Use a secant for average slope
blocks.text: The secant joins the curve at x = 1 and x = 2. Its slope is the exact curve rise divided by the horizontal step: 3a / 1 = 3a. For positive a, the curve gets steeper across this interval.

steps.text: The curve starts at {y} and ends at {endY}. Subtract the two heights: the exact curve change is {curveChange}.
The tangent uses the starting slope {slope}. Over one unit, it rises by {tangentChange}, reaching {tangentEndY}. The curve instead reaches {endY}. These are different objects.
The orange secant joins the two curve points. Its slope is {secantSlope}. It summarizes the whole interval, while the blue tangent describes the starting point.

quickQuestions: Show the tangent and secant. Why are their slopes different?
Add a comparison of the exact curve change and tangent change.
If a is 5, is the curve change 10 or 15? Explain carefully.

quiz.question: For a = 1, which changes are exact on x = 1 to x = 2?

options.text: The curve rises 2 and the tangent rises 3.
The curve rises 3 and the tangent rises 2.
Both rise 2 because the derivative is 2.

quiz.explanation: f(2) − f(1) = 4 − 1 = 3. The tangent L(x) = 2x − 1 rises from 1 to 3, so its change is 2.

pages.eyebrow: 03 / KNOW THE LIMIT OF THE MODEL
pages.title: Local does not mean linear everywhere.
pages.summary: A useful approximation has a scope. Explain the difference before trusting the prediction.

blocks.title: Spot the misconception
blocks.text: A derivative of 2 at one point does not make a whole curve linear. For f(x) = x² the derivative is 2x, so its value changes as x changes.

blocks.title: Account for the missing term
blocks.text: At x = 1 + h, the curve is a + 2ah + ah². The tangent gives a + 2ah. Their difference is ah². For our unit step h = 1, the gap is a.
blocks.formula: f(1 + h) − L(1 + h) = a h²

blocks.title: Use the model with a check
blocks.text: Name the interval and the object: curve or tangent. State whether a number is a local slope, an average slope, or an exact change. Smaller steps make the absolute gap ah² smaller, but do not make it identically zero when a and h are nonzero.

steps.text: The local slope is {slope}, but the slope of the curve varies with x. One derivative value does not turn a curved function into a straight line.
Our unit step leaves a gap of {error} between the curve and its tangent. The curve changes by {curveChange}; the tangent changes by {tangentChange}. The difference is the quadratic term.
Before using a slope, ask three questions. Which object am I describing? Which interval am I using? Is this a local rate or an exact finite change? Try explaining the distinction in your own words.

quickQuestions: Show two comparison cards and explain why a local slope does not make the curve linear.
Derive the error ah² step by step and add a note.
Quiz me on local slope versus exact change without giving the answer first.

quiz.question: Why does the tangent underestimate this curve at x = 2?

options.text: A slope can never describe a curve.
The tangent omits the positive quadratic term a h².

quiz.explanation: The tangent retains the constant and linear terms. For positive a and h = 1, the omitted quadratic term is a, exactly the gap in the two endpoint values.
